title: Dead Money Decade: Hedge Fund Tactics Outshine Bonds for Long-Term Gains
body:
Investors are being urged to reconsider the long‑standing reliance on government bonds as the cornerstone of a balanced portfolio, with a growing chorus of analysts pointing to managed‑futures strategies as a more resilient alternative in an era of persistently low yields and heightened volatility. The argument, championed by former Deutsche Bank International (DBi) economist Andrew Beer, suggests that a modern twist on the classic 60/40 equity‑bond split—by allocating a portion of the “bond” side to systematic, trend‑following futures—could generate higher risk‑adjusted returns while preserving the defensive qualities investors seek from fixed‑income assets.

The case against traditional bonds has sharpened over the past decade as central banks worldwide have driven policy rates to historic lows, compressing yields on sovereign debt to levels that barely outpace inflation. Even as interest rates begin to climb, the upside potential for bond portfolios remains limited, and the sector has shown a propensity to underperform during periods of rapid rate hikes or unexpected macro shocks. Moreover, the “dead money” label—referring to assets that generate little real return—has become a common refrain among portfolio managers who see bond holdings as a drag on overall performance, especially when equity markets are buoyant.

Managed futures, by contrast, employ a rules‑based approach that seeks to capture price momentum across a diverse array of asset classes, including commodities, currencies, equity indices, and interest‑rate contracts. The strategy is inherently uncorrelated with traditional equities and bonds, offering a potential hedge against market dislocations. Proponents argue that systematic trend following can thrive in both inflationary and deflationary environments, as it simply rides the direction of price movements regardless of the underlying cause. Historical back‑testing by industry groups shows that a modest allocation—typically 5 to 15 percent of a portfolio—to managed futures can enhance Sharpe ratios and reduce drawdowns, especially when combined with a conventional equity exposure.

Critics caution that managed‑futures funds are not a panacea. Their performance can be highly dependent on the quality of the underlying models, the discipline of the trading team, and the cost structure associated with frequent turnover. Additionally, the strategy’s reliance on liquidity can be tested during extreme market stress, when futures contracts may experience widening spreads or reduced depth. Nevertheless, the growing assets under management in the space—now exceeding $400 billion globally—reflects a widening acceptance among institutional investors who view systematic diversification as a complement rather than a replacement for bonds.

From a practical standpoint, integrating managed futures into a traditional 60/40 framework could be achieved through low‑cost exchange‑traded funds (ETFs) or through dedicated mandates offered by hedge‑fund managers. Advisors are urged to conduct thorough due diligence, focusing on track records that span multiple market cycles and on risk‑management protocols that limit exposure to any single sector or contract. The shift also invites a reevaluation of portfolio construction philosophies, moving away from static asset‑class allocations toward dynamic, factor‑based exposures that can adapt to evolving macro conditions.

Looking ahead, the pressure on bond markets is unlikely to abate. With fiscal deficits expanding and central banks navigating the delicate balance between curbing inflation and supporting growth, yields may remain volatile for the foreseeable future. As such, the appeal of a systematic, trend‑following overlay—capable of delivering upside in rising‑rate environments while dampening downside risk—could gain further traction. Investors who act now to diversify away from “dead money” and incorporate managed‑futures exposure may find themselves better positioned to navigate the uncertainties of the next decade, achieving a more robust risk‑adjusted return profile without abandoning the defensive intent that bonds have traditionally provided.
